# Session 4 — Enrichment and clustering {#sec-enrich}
[Wednesday 30-09 afternoon]{.session-chip}

You now have thousands of significant genes, which is not an answer to a biological
question. Enrichment analysis turns that list into statements about **function**.
The enrichment tests and clustering use base R — `phyper`, `fisher.test`,
`p.adjust`, `kmeans` — with the DESeq2 results and transformed expression values
from Session 3. The setup below recreates those objects in a fresh R session.

::: {.run-local}
**Start here after restarting R.** Run this entire block, from top to bottom,
before §4.1. It does not require any R objects from an earlier session. It reloads
the counts, repeats the Session 3 model fit, and creates both the results table
for enrichment and the transformed expression values for clustering.

**Required file:** the count table from `C_fructicola_counts.zip` must be at
`~/work/module2/C_fructicola_counts/GSE103878_1104.genes.count.txt`. If it is
missing, upload and unpack that zip from Absalon into `~/work/module2` first.
The extra annotation file, `gene_sets.csv`, is downloaded below if needed.

```r
library(DESeq2)

# 1. Check the count file and fetch the gene-set annotations if needed
count_file <- "~/work/module2/C_fructicola_counts/GSE103878_1104.genes.count.txt"
if (!file.exists(count_file)) {
  stop("Count file missing: upload and unpack C_fructicola_counts.zip into ~/work/module2, then rerun this setup.")
}
if (!file.exists("~/work/module2/gene_sets.csv")) {
  download.file("https://mutwil.github.io/bigdata-module2-transcriptomics/data/gene_sets.csv",
                "~/work/module2/gene_sets.csv")
}

# 2. Read the counts and identify the condition of each sample
countdata <- read.delim(count_file, row.names = 1)
coldata <- data.frame(
  row.names = colnames(countdata),
  condition = factor(sub("[0-9]+$", "", colnames(countdata)))
)

# 3. Rebuild and fit the same DESeq2 model used in Session 3
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = countdata,
                              colData   = coldata,
                              design    = ~ condition)
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10, ]
dds <- DESeq(dds)

# 4. Create the APP-versus-CON results table for enrichment
fdr_cutoff <- 0.05
res <- results(dds,
               contrast = c("condition", "APP", "CON"),
               alpha = fdr_cutoff)

# 5. Create the transformed expression values needed for clustering in §4.7
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)

# 6. Check that the setup finished successfully
head(res)
dim(assay(vsd))
```

**Wait for the whole block to finish before continuing.** `DESeq()` prints
progress messages while fitting the model. At the end, you should see the first
rows of `res` and the dimensions of the transformed matrix (genes × 12 samples).
If you see an error, resolve that first rather than proceeding to §4.1.

You now have `coldata` (sample conditions), `dds` (the fitted model), `res`
(APP-versus-CON results), `fdr_cutoff` (the 5% FDR target), and `vsd` (transformed
expression values for clustering). Your files persist under `~/work/module2`;
rerun this setup whenever you restart R. **No need to return to Session 3.**
:::

## 4.1 The gene list, the universe, and the sets

```r
gene_sets <- read.csv("~/work/module2/gene_sets.csv")
head(gene_sets, 3)
sort(table(gene_sets$term_name), decreasing = TRUE)

universe <- rownames(res)[!is.na(res$padj)]    # genes with an available adjusted p-value
de_genes <- rownames(res)[!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < fdr_cutoff & res$log2FoldChange > 2]
length(universe); length(de_genes)
```

The threshold (`log2FC > 2`) is a **choice you are making** — §4.6 shows how much it
matters.

## 4.2 Are P450 genes over-represented?

Our question is: **does our upregulated gene list contain more Cytochrome P450
genes than we would expect from a random list of the same size?**

The **hypergeometric test** answers this question. It uses the same idea as the
[random-draw simulator](#sec-enrichment-simulator), but calculates the probability
directly instead of drawing 100 random lists. You do not need to calculate a
formula by hand: we will give R the sizes of the background, our list, and their
overlap with the P450 family.

### Find the P450 genes

```r
# Identify annotation rows labelled "Cytochrome P450"
p450_rows <- gene_sets$term_name == "Cytochrome P450"

# Take the gene IDs from those rows
p450_genes <- gene_sets$gene[p450_rows]

# Count each gene only once, even if its annotation appears more than once
p450_genes <- unique(p450_genes)

# Keep only P450 genes that belong to our analysis background
p450_genes <- p450_genes[p450_genes %in% universe]

head(p450_genes)
```

**Read the R:** `==` checks whether two values are equal. `p450_rows` therefore
contains `TRUE` for P450 rows and `FALSE` for other rows. Square brackets keep the
entries marked `TRUE`. `%in%` asks whether each gene ID occurs in another list;
it does not calculate a percentage.

### Count the genes, then compare observed with expected

```r
# How many genes are in the background and in our upregulated list?
background_size <- length(universe)
list_size <- length(de_genes)

# How many background genes belong to the P450 family?
set_size <- length(p450_genes)

# For each upregulated gene, ask: is it a P450 gene?
is_p450 <- de_genes %in% p450_genes

# Count the TRUE answers: this is our observed overlap
overlap <- sum(is_p450)

# Display the four numbers used by the test
background_size
list_size
set_size
overlap
```

`length()` counts entries in a list of gene IDs. `sum(is_p450)` counts the `TRUE`
answers because R treats `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE` as 0.

If P450 genes make up 1% of the background, a random list of 300 genes would
contain **3 P450 genes on average**. Use the actual proportions in our data:

```r
# Fraction of background genes that are P450 genes
background_fraction <- set_size / background_size

# Expected P450 count in a random list of the same size as ours
expected_overlap <- list_size * background_fraction

# Fold enrichment = observed P450 count / expected P450 count
fold_enrichment <- overlap / expected_overlap

overlap
expected_overlap
fold_enrichment
```

A fold enrichment of **1** means observed and expected counts are equal; **2**
means twice as many P450 genes as expected. This describes the size of the
enrichment, **not whether it is statistically significant**.

### Ask whether the overlap is surprising

We now ask: **if we selected genes randomly from the background, how often would
we get our observed number of P450 genes or more?**

```r
# Number of background genes that are NOT P450 genes
other_size <- background_size - set_size

# Probability of obtaining our observed P450 count or MORE by chance
p_value <- phyper(
  q = overlap - 1,     # include the observed overlap itself (explained below)
  m = set_size,        # P450 genes available in the background
  n = other_size,      # non-P450 genes available in the background
  k = list_size,       # number of genes selected in each random list
  lower.tail = FALSE  # ask for counts ABOVE q
)

p_value
```

**Why subtract 1?** With `lower.tail = FALSE`, R answers **"more than q"**.
If we observed 10 P450 genes, we want **10 or more**, so we ask for **more than 9**.
That is all `overlap - 1` does. Here `q`, `m`, `n` and `k` are R's argument names;
the comments explain what to supply to each one.

A small p-value means an overlap this large would be unusual under random
selection. It does not measure the size of the enrichment. This is one gene-set
test; we will adjust for testing many sets in §4.4. See the
[R reference for `phyper()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/Hypergeometric.html).

*Check your understanding:* if the observed overlap were 6, what number should
we supply as `q` to include 6, 7, 8, and all larger possible overlaps?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Use `q = 5`. More than 5 means 6 or more. The code already does this using
`q = overlap - 1`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: the same test using Fisher's exact test"}
We can put the same gene counts into a table. Rows separate selected genes from
the remaining background genes; columns separate P450 from non-P450 genes.
This is an alternative calculation, not an extra test you need to perform.

```r
comparison <- rbind(
  Selected = c(P450 = overlap,
               Other = list_size - overlap),
  Not_selected = c(P450 = set_size - overlap,
                   Other = other_size - (list_size - overlap))
)
comparison

# "greater" asks whether P450 genes are over-represented in the selected list
fisher.test(comparison, alternative = "greater")$p.value
```

This gives the same p-value as the hypergeometric calculation above, apart from
possible numerical rounding.
:::

## 4.3 Check the method with a deliberately enriched list

Before interpreting the real result, we will make an **artificial gene list**
with an unusually high proportion of P450 genes. This is a *positive control*:
a test case in which we deliberately build in the pattern we want to detect.

We will select **60 P450 genes and 240 other genes**, giving 300 genes in total.
P450 genes will therefore make up **60/300 = 20%** of this artificial list.
Compare that with `background_fraction` from §4.2: 20% should be much higher for
our course data. We keep the same background and do not change the real
`de_genes` list.

### Prepare two separate pools of genes

`p450_genes` already contains the background P450 genes from §4.2. We now need
a second pool containing the other background genes.

```r
# Mark which background genes are P450 genes
is_p450_background <- universe %in% p450_genes

# ! means "not": keep the background genes that are NOT P450 genes
other_genes <- universe[!is_p450_background]

# Check the pool sizes: we need at least 60 P450 and 240 other genes
length(p450_genes)
length(other_genes)
```

### Build the artificial list

```r
# Make the random selections reproducible when we rerun this example
set.seed(1)

# Choose 60 different P450 genes
chosen_p450 <- sample(p450_genes, size = 60, replace = FALSE)

# Choose 240 different non-P450 genes
chosen_other <- sample(other_genes, size = 240, replace = FALSE)

# Join the two selections into one artificial list
control_genes <- c(chosen_p450, chosen_other)

# Check its total size and its P450 overlap
control_size <- length(control_genes)
control_overlap <- sum(control_genes %in% p450_genes)
control_size       # 300 genes in total
control_overlap    # 60 of them are P450 genes
```

**Read the R:** `sample()` randomly chooses gene IDs from a pool. `size` says how
many to choose, and `replace = FALSE` prevents choosing the same gene twice.
`c()` joins the two selections. `set.seed(1)` makes the random choices repeatable
for the same inputs; **1 is just a seed label**, not the number of genes to select.
The identities are random, but the counts are fixed because we requested exactly
60 P450 and 240 other genes.

### Test the artificial list in the same way

```r
# Expected P450 count if all 300 genes had been drawn randomly from the background
control_expected <- control_size * background_fraction

# Compare the 60 P450 genes we deliberately included with that expectation
control_fold <- control_overlap / control_expected

# Same test as before, but using the artificial list's size and overlap
control_pvalue <- phyper(
  q = control_overlap - 1,  # ask for 60 or more, by asking for more than 59
  m = set_size,            # same background P450 pool as before
  n = other_size,          # same background non-P450 pool as before
  k = control_size,        # now selecting a list of 300 genes
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

control_expected
control_fold
control_pvalue
```

You should find a large fold enrichment and a small p-value: the test detects the
P450 enrichment we deliberately created. This is a **check of the calculation**,
not a biological discovery and not proof that every part of the analysis is
correct. A non-significant result for the real list can still be a valid outcome.

## 4.4 Test every category

```r
# Background and selected-list sizes stay the same for every category
N <- length(universe)
n <- length(de_genes)

res_enrich <- data.frame()
for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
  sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
  K  <- sum(sg %in% universe)
  k  <- sum(de_genes %in% sg)
  if (K < 5) next
  res_enrich <- rbind(res_enrich, data.frame(
    term = tm, set_size = K, overlap = k,
    expected = round(n * K / N, 2),
    fold     = round(k / (n * K / N), 2),
    pvalue   = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, n, lower.tail = FALSE)))
}
res_enrich$padj <- p.adjust(res_enrich$pvalue, method = "BH")   # adjust for testing multiple gene sets
res_enrich <- res_enrich[order(res_enrich$pvalue), ]

head(res_enrich, 12)
sum(res_enrich$pvalue < 0.05)      # raw
sum(res_enrich$padj  < 0.05)       # after BH
```

## 4.5 Nothing is significant. Why?

This is the most common outcome of a first real enrichment analysis, and being able
to diagnose it is worth more than a lucky hit. Four things work against us here, and
you can check each one:

1. **The gene list is enormous** — ~18% of all tested genes. A list that big
   overlaps every category at roughly the background rate; enrichment needs a
   *selective* list.
2. **The categories are protein families, not biological processes.** "Protein
   kinase" is scattered across every pathway; real GO terms describe processes
   switched on together — a family has no reason to move as a block.
3. **BH still costs us** even with only ~29 categories — check the gap between the
   best raw p-value and its padj.
4. **Most of the genome has no usable annotation** — count how many of the tested
   genes appear in no category at all (`sum(!(universe %in% gene_sets$gene))`);
   they can never contribute a hit.

It would be easy to make this session produce an impressive table by hunting for a
category and threshold that happen to pass. That is p-hacking, and it is the single
most common way enrichment analysis is abused in the literature. The result above is
what this data honestly gives.

## 4.6 How much does the threshold matter?

```r
for (lfc in c(1, 2, 3)) {
  dg <- rownames(res)[!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange > lfc]
  out <- data.frame()
  for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
    sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
    K  <- sum(sg %in% universe); k <- sum(dg %in% sg)
    if (K < 5) next
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(term = tm,
                 p = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, length(dg), lower.tail = FALSE)))
  }
  out <- out[order(out$p), ]
  cat(sprintf("log2FC > %d (%5d genes): best raw p = %.3f | top 3: %s\n",
              lfc, length(dg), min(out$p), paste(head(out$term, 3), collapse = " | ")))
}
```

The ranking reshuffles as the threshold moves — a different cut-off would have given
you a different "top hit" to write about. This is exactly the lecture's argument for
**whole-distribution methods**: GSEA ranks *every* gene and asks where a set's
members fall in that ranking, with no threshold at all. With curated annotation you
would run it with `fgsea` or `clusterProfiler`; for this genome, GO or PFAM terms
would first have to come from InterProScan or eggNOG-mapper.

## 4.7 Clustering expression profiles

Enrichment on one gene list answers one question. Clustering first, then testing
each cluster, asks *which programmes* the fungus runs in *which* growth form — the
analysis on the last slide of the lecture.

```r
conds <- c("CON", "APP", "CIH", "IL")
va    <- assay(vsd)
prof  <- sapply(conds, function(cd) rowMeans(va[, coldata$condition == cd]))

# genes that actually change, scaled to shape rather than level
vary   <- names(sort(apply(prof, 1, var), decreasing = TRUE))[1:1500]
scaled <- t(scale(t(prof[vary, ])))

set.seed(42)
km <- kmeans(scaled, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
table(km$cluster)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (i in 1:4) {
  members <- scaled[km$cluster == i, ]
  matplot(t(members[1:min(120, nrow(members)), ]), type = "l", lty = 1,
          col = adjustcolor("grey50", 0.25), xaxt = "n",
          ylab = "scaled expression",
          main = paste0("Cluster ", i, " (n = ", sum(km$cluster == i), ")"))
  lines(km$centers[i, ], col = "#C44E52", lwd = 3)
  axis(1, 1:4, conds)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

*Your turn:* run the §4.4 loop on one cluster's genes, with the 1,500 variable genes
as the universe. Do the CON-peaking cluster's top categories make biological sense?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```r
i  <- which.max(km$centers[, "CON"])          # the CON-peaking cluster
cl <- rownames(scaled)[km$cluster == i]
Nu <- length(vary); nn <- length(cl)
out <- data.frame()
for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
  sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
  K  <- sum(sg %in% vary); k <- sum(cl %in% sg)
  if (K < 5) next
  out <- rbind(out, data.frame(term = tm, overlap = k, set_size = K,
               fold = round(k / (nn * K / Nu), 2),
               p = phyper(k - 1, K, Nu - K, nn, lower.tail = FALSE)))
}
out$padj <- p.adjust(out$p, "BH")
head(out[order(out$p), ], 5)
```
A cluster is a much more coherent list than "everything with padj < 0.05" — the
folds rise, and the CON cluster leans towards cytochrome P450 and
heterokaryon-incompatibility genes (raw p ≈ 0.015). But nothing survives BH, so the
honest way to report it is as a hypothesis, never as a finding.
:::

# Appendix — Connecting to RStudio on ERDA {#sec-erda}

Everything in this module runs in RStudio on ERDA. This is how you get there.
**Do the sign-up before the first class** — it is not instant.

## 1. Get an ERDA account

ERDA is the University of Copenhagen's *Electronic Research Data Archive*. Go to
[erda.dk](https://erda.dk) and choose **"Sign up to ERDA using your KU / UCPH
account"**, then log in with your usual KU credentials. ERDA supports two-factor
authentication, so have your phone to hand.

You only need a web browser. Nothing is installed on your own machine.

## 2. Start an RStudio session

Once you are logged in to ERDA (follow along in the **R Studio on ERDA** slides in
the *General course information* module on Absalon — they show a screenshot of every
step):

1. On the ERDA home page, click the **Jupyter** app (also in the left icon bar).
2. Under **Select a Jupyter Service**, stay on the **DAG** tab (*Data Analysis
   Gateway* — the interactive service; MODI is for batch HPC jobs) and press
   **Start DAG**.
3. You land on **JupyterHub**. Press **Start My Server**.
4. Under **Server Options → Select a notebook image**, choose
   **Big Data in Biotechnology Notebook** — this is the course's own image with the
   right packages preinstalled. Do not take the default Python notebook.
5. When the launcher opens, click **RStudio** (under *Notebook*). The same launcher
   also offers **Terminal** under *Other*.

You now have RStudio running in your browser on a KU machine. Worth knowing about
DAG sessions: you get **8 cores and 16 GB of memory**, a session is **terminated
after 2 hours of inactivity**, and the machine itself is **non-persistent** — see
the next point.

## 3. One-time setup: the `module2` folder

Your ERDA files appear inside every session at `~/work` (in full:
`/home/jovyan/work/`). **Everything in this module lives in one folder inside it.**
Make it once — paste into the RStudio console:

```r
dir.create("~/work/module2", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

(Or in the ERDA file manager: right-click → New Folder → `module2`.)

That one folder is the whole convention. Every code block on this page reads and
writes `~/work/module2/...`, so once the files below are in place, every block runs
by copy-paste alone.

::: {.provenance}
**Only `~/work` survives.** In ERDA's own words, spawned instances are
non-persistent: *any change made during a session is lost once the server is
terminated — the only exception is data saved in the provided mount directory
(`~/work`)*. And sessions do terminate: after 2 hours of inactivity, automatically.
Save everything under `~/work/module2` and it is there next session.
:::

## 4. The files: Absalon → ERDA

Exercise data come from **Absalon → Module 2 — Transcriptomics**. Download the
files to your computer, then upload them into `~/work/module2` in the ERDA file
manager — **zips expand automatically on upload**, so there is nothing further to
do. (If a zip ever does arrive unexpanded, right-click it → Unpack.) Install
kallisto from the ERDA Terminal as shown in [§2.1](#sec-mapping). The CDS reference
is also downloaded automatically there, so it is not in this list of manual
downloads:

| File to download | Put in ERDA | Used in |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `C_fructicola_GSE103878_small.zip` (139 MB) | upload to `module2` → expands to `C_fructicola_GSE103878_small/` | Session 1–2 |
| `C_fructicola_counts.zip` | upload to `module2` → expands to `C_fructicola_counts/` | Session 3 |
| `gene_sets.csv` — or `download.file()` as in [§4](#sec-enrich) | straight into `module2` | Session 4 |
| `CountTable_GroupExercise2025.csv` | straight into `module2` | Assignment |
| `Annot_GroupExercise2025.csv` | straight into `module2` | Assignment |

When it is all in place, `~/work/module2` looks like this:

```
~/work/module2/
    C_fructicola_GSE103878_small/    the reads (Session 1; filtered/ appears inside)
    bin/kallisto                      the installed program (Session 2)
    GSE103878_1104.transcripts.fasta  CDS reference, downloaded automatically (Session 2)
    C_fructicola_GSE103878.idx        index you build from the FASTA (Session 2)
    results/                         your kallisto output (Session 2)
    C_fructicola_counts/             count table + annotation (Session 3)
    gene_sets.csv                    functional categories (Session 4)
    CountTable_GroupExercise2025.csv
    Annot_GroupExercise2025.csv      the assignment data
```

## 5. Find the terminal — you need it for kallisto

Session 2 runs `kallisto` from a command line, not from R. You do not need to leave
RStudio:

> In RStudio, select the **Terminal** tab, immediately to the right of the
> **Console** tab in the lower-left pane.

That gives you a real shell on your ERDA virtual machine. Alternatively, go back to
the DAG launcher and choose **Terminal** instead of RStudio.

## 6. Packages

The **Big Data in Biotechnology Notebook** image already has the packages this
course needs, including `dada2`, `DESeq2` and the tidyverse — that is the point of
picking it in step 2. On ERDA, **you never install anything.** If a package seems
missing, first check you selected the course image rather than the default one, and
otherwise tell a teacher.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Working on your own computer instead"}
Allowed, but you take on the setup yourself. Install
[R](https://cran.r-project.org/) and
[RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/), then the packages:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("dada2", "DESeq2"))
```

`kallisto` needs the binary for your operating system from the
[kallisto download page](https://pachterlab.github.io/kallisto/download) (the copy
on Absalon is the **Linux** build, for ERDA — it will not run on macOS or Windows).
Use a folder of your choosing instead of `~/work/module2` and adjust the paths at
the top of each block, but keep the same layout. The teachers can only reliably
help with the ERDA setup.
:::

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to do |
|:--|:--|
| Session will not start, or times out | Wait and try again; a stuck session usually clears. Note sessions end after 2 h of inactivity. |
| R packages missing (`library(dada2)` fails) | You started the wrong notebook image. Stop the server (JupyterHub → Home) and start it again with **Big Data in Biotechnology Notebook**. |
| Cannot see your files in RStudio | You are probably not under `~/work`. Run `getwd()`; the module folder is `~/work/module2`. |
| Work disappeared after a session ended | Only `~/work` persists. Anything saved elsewhere was on the temporary machine. |
| `kallisto: command not found` | Use the program installed for this course folder: `./bin/kallisto`. |
| A path from this page does not exist | A file from the §4 table is missing, or a zip expanded into an extra nesting level — check `~/work/module2` against the layout above. (The exercise HTMLs on Absalon use the author's own paths; the ones on this page are the canonical ones.) |
| Everything is slow | Big files (the 139 MB read set) take time to upload and expand. This is normal. |

If ERDA itself is broken rather than your code, mail **support@erda.dk** — they
usually reply within one working day.

# Appendix — Enrichment simulator {#sec-enrichment-simulator}

**Could the overlap in our gene list arise by chance?** Use this simulator to
repeat the random-sampling experiment from enrichment lecture slide 14.
It runs directly in your browser — no ERDA or R setup is needed.

[Open the enrichment simulator in a full browser window](assets/enrichment-simulator.html){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

Set **N** (all background genes), **K** (gene-set members in that background),
**n** (the number of genes selected), and **k** (the observed overlap). Each draw
selects **n different genes without replacement**. The entire background is
restored before the next draw. For RNA-seq, use genes eligible for selection as
the background, including the selected genes, rather than automatically using
every gene in the genome.

The starting example has **N = 26, K = 7, n = 4, k = 2**. Click **Animate 100
draws** to watch the simulation, or **Run 100 draws** for an instant result.
Green tiles mark draws with **two or more** gene-set members. Their fraction
estimates the one-sided enrichment p-value; compare it with the exact value
shown alongside. Click any tile to inspect that draw's genes.

```{=html}
<iframe src="assets/enrichment-simulator.html" title="Interactive enrichment simulator: 100 random gene lists" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:1000px;border:1px solid #dbe3e7;border-radius:12px;"></iframe>
```

*Try it:* run the same settings several times. Why does the simulated fraction
change while the exact p-value stays the same? Does 50% gene-set membership in
our selected list, compared with about 27% in the background, necessarily mean
significant enrichment?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Discussion"}
The lists are random, so 100 draws give a different estimate each time. The exact
probability depends only on N, K, n and k: here, **P(X ≥ 2) ≈ 0.287**. The observed
proportion is higher, but the overlap is **not significant at 0.05**. We would
expect about 29 of 100 random lists to have two or more members, although the
actual number varies. Zero extreme draws would not prove a probability of zero.
This is one gene-set test; testing many gene sets also requires multiple-testing
adjustment.
:::

# Appendix — GSEA simulator {#sec-gsea-simulator}

**Are gene-set members concentrated towards one end of a ranked gene list?**
Unlike the [threshold-based simulator above](#sec-enrichment-simulator), GSEA
uses the full ranked list rather than first selecting significant genes. This
simulator uses synthetic ranking statistics, not the course data, and runs
directly in your browser.

[Open the GSEA simulator in a full browser window](assets/gsea-simulator.html){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

Choose **Beginning**, **Middle**, **End**, or **Spread out** to position the
gene-set members. You can also click individual genes to change membership.
Start with **Unweighted** scoring: each member moves the running score up by
**1/K**, and each non-member moves it down by **1/(N − K)**. Use **Next gene**
or **Animate the walk** to follow the calculation.

The **enrichment score (ES)** is the excursion furthest from zero, keeping its
sign — not the score at the end of the list, which returns to zero. A positive
ES indicates earlier accumulation of members; a negative ES indicates later
accumulation. Neither sign alone establishes statistical significance.

To estimate a p-value, generate **100 or 1,000 random gene sets** of the same
size. In the default GSEA-style comparison:

- **Positive observed ES:** among non-negative random ES values, count the
  fraction at least as large as the observed ES.
- **Negative observed ES:** among negative random ES values, count the fraction
  at least as negative as the observed ES.

For example, if the observed ES is **+0.25**, and **all 44 positive scores** out
of 100 randomisations are at least +0.25, the estimated p-value is **44/44 = 1**,
not 44/100. The denominator counts random scores in the relevant direction.
These are single-gene-set p-values, not FDR-adjusted values.

```{=html}
<iframe src="assets/gsea-simulator.html" title="Interactive GSEA simulator: running enrichment scores and random gene sets" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:1100px;border:1px solid #dbe3e7;border-radius:12px;"></iframe>
```

*Try it:* compare Beginning, Middle and End with **N = 20, K = 4**, using
unweighted scoring. Why does the middle arrangement produce both a negative
trough and a positive peak? Then generate random sets and inspect their scores.
Switch to weighted scoring to see how the sizes of the upward steps change.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Discussion and important limits"}
Members at the beginning produce ES = +1; members at the end produce ES = −1.
With the four members exactly in the middle, eight non-members first bring the
score to −0.5, the four members raise it to +0.5, and the remaining eight
non-members return it to zero. The two excursions tie: there is no unique sign.

For a tied observation, this simulator deliberately leaves the directional
p-value blank. Select **Teaching alternative: either end, compare |ES|** to
compare the maximum absolute excursion with those from all randomisations.
This additional teaching test is **not the standard GSEA nominal p-value**.

Randomisation keeps the ranks and gene-set size fixed but changes membership;
it is not sample-label permutation. The simulator does not calculate NES or FDR.
Repeating the simulation changes the p-value estimate; 100 random sets give
only a rough estimate. Zero extreme random scores does not prove a probability
of zero. See the [GSEA user guide](https://docs.gsea-msigdb.org/GSEA/GSEA_User_Guide/)
for the full method.
:::
